chapter_theme: Songs at Palani (பழநி), third part, two of them at Thiru Avinankudi at the hill's foot: the poet confesses a life spent on women and courtesans who sell themselves, begging at patrons' doors, the foul and diseased body, and the clamour of rival schools, and asks for Murugan's feet and teaching; the praise makes Murugan the Tamil child of Pukali whom Parvati fed, the lover of Valli, Siva's teacher, and the form of A, U and M.
structure_note: All follow the two halves. The confessions are mostly of women (135 to 137, 139 to 144, 147, 148); 134 runs from the womb to begging, 138 is about the rival schools, and 145 and 146 dwell on the body's filth and disease. 143 and 144 end at Thiru Avinankudi (திருவாவினன்குடி), 140, 145 and 146 at Sivamalai or Sivagiri, named for the Palani hill. 141 has a long passage of drum syllables, and 147 is a word-play song repeating one word in different senses.

134.reading: The poet traces his life from the womb through growing up and learning many arts, then being kicked on the chest by dark-haired women's feet and wasting in grief, never thinking daily 'Hara Hara Sivaya', knowing nothing of the six religions, and standing every day without shame at the gates of those who give food; he asks whether he will perish so. The praise names Murugan as nephew of Ranganatha on the serpent and of Vishnu who measured the world, the lamp of both lines and lion of honoured poets who came to Pukali that day, and Kumaresa raised by the grace of the Lord who went once as messenger to Paravai's house, at Palani.
134.nuance: The life runs from கருவின் உரு to begging at food-givers' doors (அசனமிடுவார்கள் ... தலைவாசல்), with women in the middle. உபயகுல தீப ... விருதுகவி ராஜசிங்க ... புகலியூரில் அன்று வருவோனே identifies Murugan with Sambandar, born at Pukali (Sirkazhi). The messenger to Paravai is Siva sent by Sundarar to his wife, so the praise gathers the Tamil saints round Murugan.

135.reading: The poet repeats the questions men ask about women, whether the eyes are vel or carp, the words honey or milk, the hair cloud or forest, the breasts Meru or tusks, the waist a thread, and whether the Creator did not draw them so; he asks not to drown in the maya of such women's eyes, and promises to study Murugan's poems if given a life free of trouble. The praise is a string of rhyming names: Visakha, joy of the elephant-reared girl, husband of the hunters' daughter, younger brother of Vallabha's husband, ageless god, lord of sweet knowledge, Kumara of Palani on the peacock.
135.nuance: இருகண் மாயையில் மூழ்காதே: maya here is the enchantment of the eyes. The cure offered is reading: உனது காவிய நூல் ஆராய்வேன், I will study the poems about you. Two words are corrupt, and the women's or the man's voice in the questions is not clear to me.

136.reading: The poet speaks of courtesans whose quarrelsome carp eyes make war as Kama's army, sinful, angry women who speak ever so sweetly, and asks for grace so that his mind will not wander daily thinking union with them is sweet. The praise names Murugan the lover who embraced Valli till she melted, the giver of favours to Vedic Brahmins, the teacher who spoke the Pranava into the ear of the moon-crowned Siva, the enemy of the demons, and the pure guru whose twelve eyes give grace and who delights in his devotees, at Palani Sivagiri among groves and fields.
136.nuance: செவியிற் பிரணவம் ஓதிய தேசிக names the Om story outright. The praise calls Murugan himself காமுகன், the lover, for Valli, in the same song that confesses desire for courtesans; I read the contrast as deliberate, love given to the god against love sold.

137.reading: The poet describes at length lovemaking with women ready to sell their breasts, drinking from their lips, hair loosening, the waist bending and the forehead mark smudged, and asks whether he must fade in the great pool of cruel infatuation. The praise names Kandavel who bowed at the lotus feet of the hunter girl, the vel that dried the seven seas and shattered the mountain, and Murugan who gladly accepted the milk of the mountain's daughter, bidden to sing Tamil praised in every direction, at Palani.
137.nuance: கனதனம் விற்கச் சமைந்த, ready to sell their breasts, marks them as courtesans. The milk from the breast of the mountain's daughter given with செந்தமிழ் பகர் is the story told of Sambandar, fed by Parvati before he sang; the song gives it to Murugan. As in 15, Murugan bows before Valli (பதம் பணிந்தருள்).

138.reading: The poet lists the schools that clamour with their many books, the Buddhists, the ritualists, the Turks, the followers of Kapila and Kanada, the materialists, the quarrelling logicians and the left-hand Bhairavas, and asks whether there will be a day when Murugan makes clear the teaching that is hard for anyone to discern, gives him the vision of knowledge and grants him his feet. The praise names the vel thrown at the elephant-faced demon and the horse-faced and lion-faced warriors while ghouls and Bhadrakali danced, the chest that rests on the hunter girl's breasts, and Palani, which rises to the rain clouds.
138.nuance: The list names Islam (துருக்கர்) beside the Indian schools, as one more voice in the dispute. The plea is for உபதேசம் and ஞான தரிசனம்: not to win the debate but to be taught past it. காம கருமிகள் may be the ritualists of desire-rites; that identification is mine.

139.reading: The poet describes courtesans who bare their sandal-smeared breasts, show a jasmine smile, let flowers fall from loosened hair like stars, stand and name a price, and once the money is in their hands open their garments and press close, and asks whether he will waste away for them. The praise names Murugan the guru who told the sweet meaning to Siva of the crescent, konrai and serpent, brother of the elephant-faced god, the one who grants his feet on the poet's head, the child who drank at Uma's breast when she lifted him, and the lover of the hunters' daughter at Sivagiri.
139.nuance: விலைகூறி, naming the price, and முதல் உளது கைப்புகுந்து, once the capital is in hand, make the trade plain. எனது தலையில் பதங்கள் அருள்வோனே, who grants his feet on my head, is the poet speaking of a gift already given, the feet set on the devotee's head.

140.reading: The poet describes women with flowered hair, brow-mark, arrow-eyes, conch necks, breasts and a creeper-thin waist, cuckoo voices and the gait of peahens and swans, women who seize a man's wealth and spread nets, and asks whether he will give up the base pleasure of following them in the burning mire. The praise names Murugan the guru of Sambhu, who holds axe and deer and wears konrai, thumbai, moon, river and snake; the vel that boiled the sea and laid the demons and mountains to sleep; the feet on the whirling peacock; and the husband of the hunter girl, daughter of Lakshmi and daughter-in-law of Uma, at Sivamalai.
140.nuance: பொருள்பறி, seizing wealth, and புலையவர் வழி இன்பு, the pleasure of the base path, carry the judgement. திருமகள் ... குறத்தி மகள், making Valli Lakshmi's daughter, follows the tradition of her birth. The opening words of Siva's description (பறித்த விழி) I cannot place, and the long description of the women has compressed lines.

141.reading: The poet describes women who stand every day at the doorway with breasts like golden pots, setting a price so that all may have their pleasure, and confesses that, bewildered by their tricks, he has wasted in desire on the bed and drowned in a sea of pleasure; he asks Murugan to remove his deceitful heart and give him the refuge of his feet. The praise is a long passage of drum syllables, the peacock dancing so that the elephants of the eight directions and the cosmic sphere tremble, and the vel that killed the demon's kin, at Palani.
141.nuance: அனைவரும் கொளும் என்று மேவு இலையிடும், setting a price so that all may take, is the common woman of Kural chapter 92. The deceit confessed is the poet's own (வஞ்சக நெஞ்சு) as well as the women's (தோதகம்). The drum syllables (தனதனந்தன, டிகுகு, டுண்டுடு) are rhythm.

142.reading: The poet describes the breasts of women who delight in fine garments, and says that, melting like wax in fire for them and sunk in the sea of birth with debased words, he is like a fool to be laughed at; he asks whether he must be bound to the shame of this infatuation. The praise names Guha whose shoulders bear the scent of the hunter girl's breasts, the lord who gave delight to the mountain king's daughter, consort of the ascetic Siva with the river in his hair, the vel that destroyed the demons in an instant, and Kumara of Palani.
142.nuance: அனற்குள் மெழுக்கென, like wax in fire, and பவக்கடல், the sea of births, set the infatuation within the round of births. The song's syllables are packed tightly into its rhythm, and several word-splits in both halves, especially the last two lines, are my guesses.

143.reading: The poet says that after embracing women with breasts rising like mountains and anointed with camphor, he lost the wealth in his hand and grew weary, his mind failing, hiccups rising, dried out like ginger, and asks whether, leaving this wasting disease, he will praise Murugan as his treasure. The praise names him the old man who loved the golden hunter girl given by the forest hunters, the fierce hero whose vel shattered the seas, the mountain and Sura's heads, the gracious one whose small feet ring with anklet bells, and the son of Sankari, at Thiru Avinankudi.
143.nuance: கைப்பொருளே இழந்து, losing the wealth in the hand, links the women to the man's ruin. சுக்கதுபோலே, like dried ginger, is the body after. அக்கிழவோனே, that old man, is Murugan's disguise as an old man to win Valli.

144.reading: The poet says that, his heart wavering with a love bound to deeds and bearing a false body of flesh, blood, skin and fat, he has bowed at the feet of women with flowered hair, sharp eyes and bow brows and desired their golden shoulders, and asks whether it is right for him to sink so low and perish. The praise names the vel that fought until Sura fell and the waters dried while the gods stood worshipping, the one who roams the hill field where the pure hunter peahen stood, the one dear to the Lord who drank the poison, whom Brahma and Garuda-bannered Vishnu worship, at Thiru Avinankudi among sugar mills and groves.
144.nuance: தாள் பணிந்து, bowing at their feet, is worship given to the wrong feet, and தாழ்வடைந்து உலைய, sinking and perishing, is its result. பொய்க் காயம், the false body, is listed as flesh, blood, skin and fat.

145.reading: The poet calls the body a hut of excrement, urine, fat, bone, flesh, guts, hair and blood, and those who live in it cruel, ignorant and pathless; calling himself hellish and wretched, he says he will not forget the smiling faces, shining eyes and two flower feet of Murugan, who came on the peacock so that he might hold in his mind 'Saravana' and the light of Siva. The praise names Murugan lord of the land of Puliyur, where cuckoos and bees sound in the groves and peacocks dance, the one who sent the asuras with their elephants and horses to Yama's city, guru of the Lord whose dancing feet Brahma, sages, gods and Rambha hail with 'Hara Hara Siva Siva', and the lover of the hunter girl at Sivamalai.
145.nuance: குரம்பை, the hut, is the body, as in Saiva poetry generally. The string of names for himself (நரகனை, கலியனை, சடலனை) is the poet's self-abuse before the grace. புலிநகர் is Puliyur, Chidambaram, the dancer's city. The middle lines are hard to construe, and whether the cruel ones are all who live in bodies or the women is my reading.

146.reading: The poet describes the body, oozing blood, filth and urine, with worms writhing, flesh, marrow and phlegm, as a house whose tenants are diseases, fits, colic, headache and stomach-ache, and confesses he has cherished it and been infatuated with women; he asks that his grief and deeds be scattered and that Murugan place his feet on his head. The praise names the vel that pierced the mountain and burned the sea, the peacock rider whom gods and sages hail as guru and refuge, the son of the mountain's daughter, sister of Hari, and the one whom the hunter girl embraced in fear when Ganapati came as an elephant, at Palani.
146.nuance: குடிகள் எனப் பல ... பிணி: the diseases are the body's tenants. The plea is the same as 139's, the feet on the head (எனது தலை பதம் அருள்வாயே). The elephant that frightened Valli into Murugan's arms is told outright (கணபதி ... மதகரி வடிவு கொடு வர).

147.reading: The poet lists the things women's hair, brows, lips, teeth, ears, words, breasts and eyes are compared to, and asks whether he, a dog, should go on telling women false ways and be uselessly troubled. The praise is word play: Murugan the peacock hero by whose grace the deeds of those who bow at his anklets come loose, the nephew of Lakshmi's lord, the vel that pierced the mountain and the demons, Muruga Visakha of the Palani hill, lord of the gods whom the sea-coloured Hari praises.
147.nuance: The second half is a yamakam: கழல், கமலை, பழநி மலை and பரவை are each repeated three times with different word-splits and senses (கழல் as anklet and as coming loose). பழநி may play on பழம் நீ, the fruit story, but the text gives only the repeated word. நாயேன், I the dog, is the self-abuse. Several of the splits are uncertain.

148.reading: The poet describes lovemaking with women whose hair slips, words falter, eyes roll, throats make sounds, breasts and thighs sway and who take the upper place, and asks whether he will be troubled in that infatuation. The praise names Murugan as the one who wears the bright, sweet poetry spoken by Arunagiri, son of the pure virgin goddess Gauri who walks in the forest, and the one whose form is the A, U and M at the end of the ancient Veda, at Palani among fields, areca, plantain and jack.
148.nuance: அருணகிரி சொல் ... அணிவோனே: the poet names himself, and his poem as Murugan's ornament. பழைய மறையின் முடிவில் அகர மகர உகர படிவ வடிவம் makes Murugan the form of Om, the end of the Veda. விஜயகிரி is perhaps another name of the poet or of Palani.

links.note: Both confess begging from patrons: 15 praises them in Tamil with a wounded heart, 134 stands without shame at the gates of those who give food. 134 sets the begging at the end of a life that runs from the womb through women.

Both reject the poets' comparisons for a woman's eyes as carp, spear and the like: the Naladiyar ascetic answers them with the eye as a scooped-out palm fruit, 135 asks not to drown in their maya and turns to studying Murugan's poems.

Tirumular says that if one knows how to reach the inner light there is no quarrel at all; 138 lists the clamouring schools and asks for the teaching and vision of knowledge that would end the dispute for him.
Both open with the sects that cannot agree and ask Murugan for knowledge and his feet instead; 124 adds the ash, 138 names the schools one by one.

The Kural's பொதுநலத்தார், women whose favours are common to all, are 141's women who set a price so that all may take their pleasure; the Kural says the wise will not touch them, 141 confesses that he did.
The Kural calls the soft shoulders of women who draw no line the mire in which base men sink; 144 confesses to desiring those golden shoulders and sinking low (தாழ்வடைந்து).

Both list the body's contents, guts, fat, blood, bone and flesh. The Naladiyar asks where among them the garlanded woman is; 145 applies the list to the body the poet himself lives in, and answers with the Lord's grace.
Both give Murugan a deed of Sambandar: 132 the impaling of the Jains, 137 the milk of Parvati given to the child who then sang Tamil.

source_issues: Song 135: one corrupt character in பா஡ண (line 9); possibly பாரீர் (look!), taking ஡ண for ரீ, but uncertain.
Song 135: a stray character ஧ in மாயையி ஧ல்முழ் காதே (line 10); probably மாயையில் மூழ்காதே.
Song 146: one corrupt character in உடலு஡டே (line 3); clearly உடலூடே.
